COMMENTS: Topogaro 2, part of the Goa Topogaro cave complex in Central Sulawesi, preserves deposits up to 3 m deep, with occupations dated from about 29 ka to the Metal Age. Excavations yielded lithic flakes of chert. Use-wear analysis indicates activities such as plant processing, bone working, and butchering. Occupation was episodic, with gaps during the LGM but renewed use in the Post-LGM, Holocene, and later periods.

BIBLIOGRAPHY: Hidayat, R., & Muliarsa, I. W. (2013). Bulletin Umulolo: Media informasi pelestarian cagar budaya (Vol. 1, No. 3). Balai Pelestarian Cagar Budaya Gorontalo.
COMMENTS: The only evidence and remains of burial activity in Pamona Cave that can still be found today are a distribution of human skeletal anatomy, several wood fragments suspected to be part of burial containers (yumu), mollusk shells, and beads associated with several human skeletal parts and teeth. Most of the human skeletal remains scattered throughout the cave are incomplete, and some of the bones are extremely fragile. The parts of the human skeleton that can still be identified by examining intact anatomical features of the human skeleton are divided into two parts: 1) the axial skeleton, consisting of the skull (cranium), face, spine, and rib cage. 2) the appendicular skeleton, consisting of the shoulder blades and collarbones.

COMMENTS: Types of archaeological remains are found in the niche and cave in the form of coffins or in local language called yumu and various piles of skulls inside the coffins, most of which have decayed and scattered irregularly. Most of the skeletons remain intact, visible from the skull shape of the head and face, teeth, ribs, shoulder blades, and femur bones. The coffins found in the niche and cave have two parts: the coffin cover and the body storage container. The coffins average have a long shape with dimensions 100 cm long and 45 cm wide. Overall, the coffin dimensions from the cover to the storage container are round. Each part of both ends of the cover and body storage container has elongated carving protruding upward and downward. The carving functions as a lock for both parts of the coffin from a wooden stick or a place to tie black fiber rope.

COMMENTS: At the Tadulako Site (Doda Village), a test pit in one kalamba produced finds of human skeletal and skull fragments, teeth, pottery sherds, an ike stone (bark-beater), and a pebble stone tool (Yuniawati 2000). From observation of the right humerus by Rokhus Due Awe, it is estimated that at least ten individuals were present in the kalamba. Dental observation by Dr. Harry Widianto indicates the teeth were burned, with very fragile roots that split easily, mostly the crowns were preserved, with enamel from cusps to cervix. Dentin was largely detached or heavily cracked, and less than 30% of roots remained. The site also yielded about 32 artifacts: one megalithic statue, nine flat stones, eight pebbles, two monoliths, one stone enclosure, one covered kalamba, and ten uncovered kalamba.

COMMENTS: Artifact finds at this site total about 95 items, including megalithic statues (5), dakon stones (14), flat stones (5), tray stones (2), incised dakon stones (2), pebbles (16), pebble clusters (4), flat tables (3), stone enclosures (9), kalamba lids (10), and kalamba containers without lids (25). Radiocarbon dating from Pokekea Site, test box TG-U'47 (charcoal from spits 6-11, close to burial jars and kalamba), yielded 2170 +/- 120 BP, calibrated to 510 BC-80 AD. Excavations show that around kalamba there are large jars (about 50 cm diameter) placed tightly and densely within a slightly elevated mound stratigraphy compared with other find spots (Siswanto 2005). These jars are interpreted as burial containers. With kalamba used as burial containers and clay burial jars also present, the provisional interpretation is that Pokekea was used for burial.

The site may have begun to be occupied at 2460 +/- 120 BP, calibrated to 831 BC-232 BC (date from Box KII, spits 4-9, near stone mortar find no. 159).
